title: VIPIN JAISWAL(A-1) versus STATE OF A.P. REP.BY PUB.PROSECUTOR
case_title: VIPIN JAISWAL v. STATE OF A.P.
high_court_outcome: Acquitted two relatives, maintained conviction of appellant
neutral_facts: The accused, the husband of the deceased, was charged with causing the death of his wife, who died from burn injuries. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was subjected to physical and mental torture by her husband and in-laws for not providing sufficient dowry. The accused claimed that his wife had left behind a suicide note stating that she committed suicide due to harassment by her parents, not by her husband or in-laws. The court also found that the suicide note, written by the deceased, cast doubt on the prosecution's claim of harassment and cruelty.
offence_severity: Minimum 10 years, Maximum 20 years
physical_harm: Burn injuries
number_of_offences: Charged under 2 counts, 1 upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of the appellant (DW1) and the chit (Ext. D19) written in the handwriting of the deceased, which cast a reasonable doubt on the prosecution's story of harassment or cruelty.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the prosecution witnesses (PW1 and PW4) as having made general allegations of harassment without providing specific acts of cruelty or harassment, thereby casting doubt on their credibility.
bail_history: The appellant and his family members were arrested by the police and after one month they were released on bail.
trial_duration: The FIR was lodged on 4.4.1999. The charge-sheet was submitted against the appellant and his relatives under Sections 498A and 3048 IPC. The Trial Court convicted the appellant and his relatives on 11.12.2006. The High Court upheld the conviction on 11.12.2006. The Supreme Court decided the case on 13.3.2013.
legal_representation: A.T.M. Ranga Ramanujam, Prabhakar Sharma, Dipankar Das, Devesh Singh, Shanti Kumar Jaisani, Anu Gupta for the Appellant. Mayur R. Shah, D. Mahesh Babu, Suchitra Hrangkhawl, Amjid Maqbool, Amit K. Nain, M. Bala Shivudu for the Respondent.
investigation_status: Criminal Case under Section 3048, IPC was registered. Charge-sheet was submitted against the appellant and his relatives under Sections 498A and 3048, IPC.
appeal_history: Trial Court: Convicted the appellant and his relatives under Sections 3048 and 498A, IPC. High Court: Acquitted two other relatives of the appellant but maintained the conviction of the appellant under Sections 3048 and 498A, IPC. Supreme Court: Allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court and that of the Trial Court.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution alleged that the deceased was subjected to physical and mental torture by her husband and in-laws for not getting sufficient dowry, leading to her death. They submitted that the demand of Rs.50,000/- by the appellant was a dowry demand and that the deceased was harassed and cruelly treated by the accused.
defence_argument: The appellant argued that the deceased had left behind a suicide note stating she committed suicide due to harassment by her own parents, not by the appellant or his family. He also claimed the Rs.50,000/- demand was for purchasing a computer to start a business, not a dowry demand.
legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle that for an offence under Sections 498A and 304B of the IPC to be made out, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment by the accused in connection with dowry demands.
precedent_relied_upon: Appasaheb & Anr. vs. State of Maharashtra (2007) 9 SCC 721: 2007 (1) SCR 164
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, the husband of the deceased, was charged with causing the death of his wife, who died from burn injuries. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was subjected to physical and mental torture by her husband and in-laws for not providing sufficient dowry. The accused claimed that his wife had left behind a suicide note stating that she committed suicide due to harassment by her parents, not by her husband or in-laws. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 304 and 498A of the IPC, citing harassment and cruelty. The High Court acquitted two other relatives but upheld the conviction of the accused. The Supreme Court reviewed the case, noting that the demand for Rs.50,000/- by the accused for a computer was not a dowry demand as it was not connected to the marriage. The court also found that the suicide note, written by the deceased, cast doubt on the prosecution's claim of harassment and cruelty. The court ultimately acquitted the accused, stating that the prosecution failed to prove the essential ingredients of the offenses beyond reasonable doubt.

title: VINOD JASWANTRAY VYAS (DEAD) THROUGH LRS. versus THE STATE OF GUJARAT
case_title: Vinod Jaswantray Vyas (Dead) Through Lrs. v. The State of Gujarat
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34; Arms Act s.27
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of Section 302 IPC, sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The accused, a police officer, was involved in an incident where a man surrendered at a police station. The man was later found dead in a jail. The prosecution alleged that the accused and another police officer assaulted the man in police custody, leading to his death. The victim was accompanied by his advocate and sisters. The victim was produced before a magistrate and then sent to jail, where he later died. The medical report indicated severe injuries, and the medical expert testified that the injuries were recent and would have prevented the victim from climbing stairs.
offence_severity: Minimum: 6 years rigorous imprisonment, Maximum: Life imprisonment
physical_harm: Multiple injuries including fractures, bruises, and internal injuries leading to death
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged, both finally upheld by the High Court but later overturned by the Supreme Court
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the formidable evidence of the Medical Jurist (PW-9) that the injuries were fresh and must have occurred within six to eight hours of the death, which discredits the eyewitnesses' version that the deceased was assaulted in police custody at the Amraiwadi Police Station.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PW-1, PW-2, and PW-3) as having unnatural conduct, casting doubt on the truthfulness of their testimony due to their failure to inform their advocate about the custodial torture and not approaching higher officials or the court to make a complaint.
custody_duration: Jeeva was remanded to judicial custody on 11th June, 1992 and was lodged at Sabarmati Central jail, where he died on 12th June, 1992
bail_history: A1's sentence was suspended and he was directed to be released on bail on 6th June, 2017. However, A1 passed away during the pendency of the appeal
trial_duration: Offence: 10th June, 1992; Trial judgment: 4th March, 1997; High Court decision: 13th February, 2017; Supreme Court decision: 9th July, 2024
legal_representation: Harin P. Raval, Anando Mukherjee, Ms. Ekta Bharati, Shwetank Singh, Ms. Shreya Bansal, Ms. Shrestha Narayan, Ms. Urmi H. Raval for the Appellants; Ms. Deepanwita Priyanka, Ms. Swati Ghildiyal, Ms. Devyani Bhatt for the Respondent
investigation_status: Criminal Case No. 1920 of 1993 registered; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Convicted under Section 302 IPC', 'high_court': 'Affirmed conviction but toned down to Section 304 Part I IPC', 'supreme_court': 'Acquitted both accused'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused police officers assaulted Jeeva in police custody, causing fatal injuries, and that the victim's injuries were consistent with the assault. They also emphasized the delay in filing the complaint and the lack of motive for the accused to commit the crime.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the injuries were inflicted after Jeeva was transferred to the Sabarmati Central jail, not during his detention at the Amraiwadi Police Station. They also questioned the credibility of the eyewitnesses and highlighted the medical evidence indicating the injuries were fresh and inconsistent with the alleged custodial torture.
legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle that where medical evidence contradicts ocular testimony, especially when the contradiction is so prominent that it completely undermines the eyewitness account, the medical evidence should be given precedence.
precedent_relied_upon: Sait Tarajee Khimchand and Others v. Yelamarti Satyam alias Satteyya and Others (1972) 4 SCC 562; Narbada Devi Gupta v. Birendra Kumar Jaiswal and Another [2003] Supp. 5 SCR 90 : (2003) 8 SCC 745; Bhajan Singh alias Harbhajan Singh and Others v. State of Haryana [2011] 7 SCR 1 : (2011) 7 SCC 421
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a police officer, was involved in an incident where a man surrendered at a police station. The man was later found dead in a jail. The prosecution alleged that the accused and another police officer assaulted the man in police custody, leading to his death. The victim was accompanied by his advocate and sisters. The victim was produced before a magistrate and then sent to jail, where he later died. The medical report indicated severe injuries, and the medical expert testified that the injuries were recent and would have prevented the victim from climbing stairs. The eyewitnesses' accounts were contradicted by the medical evidence, leading to the acquittal of the accused.

title: SURAJ SINGH GUJAR & ANR. versus THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ORS.
respondent: THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ORS.
case_title: Suraj Singh Gujar & Anr. v. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Sections 323, 324 and 325 r/w. s.34
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were relatives who had a dispute over land. The incident occurred on 20.05.2011, involving a minor issue regarding the tying of bullocks. The accused objected to the action, leading to an altercation. The accused and the victim later settled their dispute through a compromise deed dated 29.01.2024, wherein both parties agreed to maintain peace and harmony. The compromise was supported by affidavits from the victim's side, including the uncle of the accused, who agreed to compound the offence.
offence_severity: 3 months to 1 year of rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: Injuries caused, but the nature and severity are not specified
number_of_offences: Three offences charged under Sections 323, 324 and 325 r/w. s.34 of IPC; conviction under Sections 323, 324 and 325 r/w. s.34 set aside
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the compromise deed dated 29.01.2024, which shows that the appellants and the complainant side are close relatives and have agreed to maintain peace and harmony in society.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses by considering the affidavits filed by the private respondents, who confirmed that they have agreed to compound the offence due to the unconditional apology and familial relationship.
post_offence_conduct: The appellants are already outside jail and need not surrender.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 20.05.2011; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 26.12.2023; Supreme Court decision: 30 August 2024
legal_representation: Ms. Deeksha Saggi, Abhishek Kumar, Rituparn Uniyal, K Anil Singh, Ram Lal Roy, Advs. for the Appellants; D. S. Parmar, A.A.G., Ms. Mrinal Gopal Elker, Abhimanyu Singh-G.a., Saurabh Singh, Ms. Shruti Verma, Nayan Mishra, Shivang Jain, Satyajeet Kumar, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence awarded; High Court: Maintained conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Conviction set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellants were convicted under Sections 323, 324 and 325 read with Section 34 of the IPC and that the High Court upheld the conviction and sentence.
defence_argument: The appellants argued that they had settled the dispute with the injured persons through a compromise deed and sought permission to compound the offence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the power under Article 142 of the Constitution can be invoked to set aside convictions in non-compoundable offences in exceptional cases, considering factors such as the nature of injuries, relation between parties, and impact on society.
precedent_relied_upon: Ramgopal & Anr. v. State of M.P [2021] 6 SCR 249 : (2022) 14 SCC 531; Murali v. State [2021] 1 SCR 201 : (2021) 1 SCC 726; Manjit Singh v. State of Punjab & Anr. (2020) 18 SCC 777; Kailash Chand v. State of Rajasthan (2021) 18 SCC 534; Srinivasan Iyenger & Anr. v. Bimla Devi Agarwal & Ors. (2019) 4 SCC 456; Ramawatar v. State of M.P [2021] 10 SCR 499 : (2022) 13 SCC 635
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was not imposed as the Supreme Court set aside the conviction under Article 142 of the Constitution, considering the nature of the incident, the close familial relationship between the parties, and the agreement to maintain peace and harmony.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court weighed the close familial relationship between the parties, the nature of the incident (a minor issue), and the agreement to maintain peace and harmony in society.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the victim were relatives who had a dispute over land. The incident occurred on 20.05.2011, involving a minor issue regarding the tying of bullocks. The accused objected to the action, leading to an altercation. The accused and the victim later settled their dispute through a compromise deed dated 29.01.2024, wherein both parties agreed to maintain peace and harmony. The compromise was supported by affidavits from the victim's side, including the uncle of the accused, who agreed to compound the offence. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 323, 324, and 325 of the IPC read with Section 34. The High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court, however, set aside the conviction under its constitutional power under Article 142, considering the nature of the incident, the relationship between the parties, and the compromise agreement.

title: KRISHIKA LULLA & ORS.  versus SHYAM VITHALRAO DEVKATIA & ANR.

The case involved a dispute over whether the title of a story could be considered a literary work under copyright law.
offence_severity: Not stated
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Not stated
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the title 'Desi Boys' does not qualify as a 'literary work' under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957, and therefore, no copyright subsists in it.

trial_duration: Dates of offence not stated, trial judgment dated 22.03.2012, High Court decision not stated, Supreme Court decision dated OCTOBER 15, 2015

The accused sought to quash the criminal proceedings, which were dismissed by the trial court. title: STATE OF HARYANA versus KRLSHAN & ANR.
case_title: State of Haryana v. Krishan & Anr.
aggravating_circumstances: Sale of poisonous liquor, attempt to destroy evidence
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of culpable homicide and other charges
neutral_facts: The prosecution case centered around a tragic incident where 36 persons died and 44 persons lost their eyesight after consuming spurious liquor purchased from a licensed liquor vend. Medical evidence confirmed that the cause of death and loss of vision was due to the consumption of liquor adulterated with methyl alcohol. Victims and their relatives stated they purchased the liquor from the respondents' vend, which was corroborated by the conduct of the respondents in disposing of remaining stock after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence showing the respondents were licensed vendors and that they had knowledge of the harmful effects of the liquor they sold.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000/- each for Section 302 IPC read with Section 120B IPC; imprisonment for a term of 5 years with fine of Rs.5,000/- each for Section 328 IPC read with Section 120B IPC
physical_harm: 36 persons lost their lives and 44 persons lost their eye sight due to consumption of poisonous liquor containing methyl alcohol
number_of_offences: 48 persons were arrayed as accused; 2 were convicted, others acquitted
premeditation_planning: Yes, the respondents were aware of the disastrous consequences of selling spurious liquor and planned to make quick money
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence supported the prosecution case that the cause of death and loss of eye sight was the result of consuming spurious liquor. The victims and their relatives stated that they purchased liquor from the vends of respondents. Conduct of the respondents in throwing away remaining stock after the incident came into limelight is also a supporting piece of evidence.
witness_credibility: Such contemporary statements of those very persons who suffered loss of eye-sight immediately after the incident cannot be ignored and there is no reason to disbelieve them. Such statements also become relevant under Section 7 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
post_offence_conduct: The respondents tried to destroy remaining bottles by throwing them away in the river/canal after the tragedy struck.
trial_duration: Offence: December 1, 1980; Trial judgment: August 18, 2000; High Court decision: May 09, 2006; Supreme Court decision: June 09, 2017
legal_representation: Sanjay Kumar Tyagi, Addi. AG, Dilip Pratap, Kamal Mohan Gupta, Advs. for the Appellant; R. S. Sodhi, Sr. Adv., Harpreet Singh Sandhu, Satyapal Khushal Chand Pasi, Ms. Apama Rohatgi Jain, Mahesh Kasana, S. K. Dhingra, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction of Krishan and Som Nath; High Court: Acquittal of respondents; Supreme Court: Conviction ordered by trial court is restored
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the respondents were responsible for selling spurious liquor containing methyl alcohol, which caused the deaths of 36 persons and blindness in 44 others. The medical evidence supported this claim, and the victims and their relatives stated they purchased the liquor from the respondents' vends. The respondents' attempt to destroy remaining bottles after the incident further supported their culpability.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no evidence connecting the respondents to the consumption of methyl alcohol by the victims. They claimed the prosecution's case was based on faulty investigation and that the respondents were not directly involved in the preparation or sale of spurious liquor.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the presence of methyl alcohol in the victims' bodies, coupled with the victims' statements and the respondents' conduct, established their culpability under Section 300 IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) and Section 120B IPC (conspiracy).
precedent_relied_upon: Joseph Kurian Philip Jose v. State of Kerala [1994] 4 Suppl. SCR 122 : (1994) 6 SCC 535; Fakhruddin v. State of MP. AIR 1967 SC 1326
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution proved the respondents' culpability in selling spurious liquor containing methyl alcohol, which caused the deaths and blindness of numerous victims. The respondents' conduct, including their attempt to destroy evidence, demonstrated full knowledge of the dangerous consequences of their actions.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court weighed the respondents' greed and exploitation of vulnerable villagers, their full knowledge of the dangerous nature of the methyl alcohol, and their attempt to destroy evidence after the tragedy.
other_sentence_order: The High Court had directed the State to pay compensation of Rs.2 lakhs each to the heirs of 36 deceased persons and Rs.1.50 lakhs each to those blinded by the spurious liquor. However, the Supreme Court did not interfere with this order as the compensation had already been disbursed.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution case centered around a tragic incident where 36 persons died and 44 persons lost their eyesight after consuming spurious liquor purchased from a licensed liquor vend. Medical evidence confirmed that the cause of death and loss of vision was due to the consumption of liquor adulterated with methyl alcohol. Victims and their relatives stated they purchased the liquor from the respondents' vend, which was corroborated by the conduct of the respondents in disposing of remaining stock after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence showing the respondents were licensed vendors and that they had knowledge of the harmful effects of the liquor they sold. The trial court convicted the respondents for their involvement in the sale of spurious liquor, while the High Court initially acquitted them, citing lack of evidence. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's acquittal, finding sufficient evidence to connect the respondents to the tragedy.

title: BALU SUDAM KHALDE & ANR versus THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: BALU SUDAM KHALDE & ANR. v. THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
aggravating_circumstances: Use of dangerous weapons, multiple blows, victim was unarmed and helpless
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s. 302 r/w 34, sentenced to life imprisonment and fine
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were strangers who engaged in a verbal altercation that escalated into a physical fight. The accused used dangerous weapons, including a sickle and sword, to assault the victim. The victim sustained severe injuries, including bleeding on his head, left paw, wrist, right hand, and right shoulder, and ultimately succumbed to his injuries. The victim was taken to a hospital where he was declared dead. The prosecution presented eyewitness accounts, medical evidence, and recovery of weapons.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment / Death
physical_harm: Severe assault causing death
number_of_offences: 4 offences charged, 2 upheld
key_evidence_accepted: Oral evidence of all the three eyewitnesses PW 1, 2, 3 is consistent and there is no good reason for the Court to disbelieve the ocular version as narrated by the three eyewitnesses.
witness_credibility: The trial court as well as the High Court looked into the oral evidence of all the three eyewitnesses closely and have recorded a concurrent finding that they are reliable witnesses.
bail_history: Both the appellants were ordered to be released on bail pending the final hearing of the present appeal. The appellant No.2 was ordered to be released on bail vide order dated 01.10.2010 and the appellant No. 1 herein was ordered to be released on bail vide order dated 04.03.2013. The bail bonds furnished by them to the satisfaction of the Additional Sessions Judge, Pune in Sessions Case No. 323 of 2001 stand cancelled.
trial_duration: The FIR was lodged on 2.04.2002. The trial court passed the order of conviction and the consequence sentence dated 12.03.2003. The High Court dismissed the criminal appeal referred to above, and thereby affirmed the order of conviction and the consequence sentence dated 12.03.2003. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 29 March 2023.
legal_representation: K. L. Janjani, Pankaj Kumar Singh, Dr. Vinod Kumar Tewari, Kailash J. Kashyap, Advs. for the Appellants. Abhikalp Pratap Singh, Siddharth Dharmadhikari, Aadi tya Aniruddha Pande, Bharat Bagla, Sourav Singh, Ms. Shreya Saxena, Ms. Yamini Singh, Advs. for the Respondent.
investigation_status: First information report lodged on 2.04.2002. The dead body of the deceased was sent for post mortem. The clothes of the deceased stained with blood were collected and sent to the forensic science laboratory for chemical analysis. The scene of offence panchnama was drawn. The clothes of all the accused were collected and sent to the FSL. The discovery panchnamas were drawn in presence of the panch witnesses. The statements of various other witnesses were recorded by the police. Chargesheet filed for the offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC.
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'The trial court convicted both the appellants herein for the offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and sentenced them to suffer life imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1000/- each with the stipulation that in default of payment of the fine they would undergo rigorous imprisonment for further six months.', 'high_court': 'The High Court dismissed the criminal appeal referred to above, and thereby affirmed the order of conviction and the consequence sentence dated 12.03.2003 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Pune.', 'supreme_court': 'The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 29 March 2023.'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that a verbal altercation between the parties resulted in a fight where the first informant was assaulted on the head and the deceased suffered severe assault leading to his death. The appellants were convicted under Section 302 r/w 34 and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court upheld the order, and the oral evidence of the three eyewitnesses was found to be consistent and reliable.
defence_argument: The defence counsel suggested that the eyewitnesses' accounts were unreliable and that the accused could not be held guilty based on the prosecution's evidence. They also argued that the case might fall under Exception 4 to Section 300, which would exclude it from being considered murder.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the initial burden to prove the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt rests on the prosecution. It also emphasized that for a case to fall under Exception 4 to Section 300, all the ingredients mentioned in the exception must be found.
precedent_relied_upon: Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753; Leela Ram v. State of Haryana AIR 1995 SC 3717; Tahsildar Singh v. State of UP AIR 1959 SC 1012; Rakesh Kumar alias Babli v. State of Haryana (1987) 2 SCC 34; Tarun Bora alias Alok Hazarika v. State of Assam 2002 Cri. LJ 4076; Rajwant Singh v. State of Kerala AIR 1966 SC 1874; State of Andhra Pradesh v. Rayavarapu Punnayya and Another (1976) 4 SCC 382; Sukhar v. State of U.P. (1999) 9 SCC 507; Govind s/o Soneram v. State of M.P. (DB) 2005 Cri.LJ 1244; Parkash Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2004) 11 SCC 381
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the deceased suffered severe injuries caused by dangerous weapons applied to his vital parts, which constitutes a case under Section 302 of the IPC. The court found that the appellants inflicted multiple blows on an unarmed and helpless person, which does not fall under Exception 4 to Section 300.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The aggravating factors weighed by the court included the use of dangerous weapons on the vital parts of the body, the infliction of multiple blows on an unarmed and helpless person, and the fact that the incident occurred in the heat of the moment and was sudden.
other_sentence_order: The appellants were ordered to surrender before the Trial Court within two weeks and to serve their sentence. Their bail bonds were cancelled.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the victim were strangers who engaged in a verbal altercation that escalated into a physical fight. The accused used dangerous weapons, including a sickle and sword, to assault the victim. The victim sustained severe injuries, including bleeding on his head, left paw, wrist, right hand, and right shoulder, and ultimately succumbed to his injuries. The victim was taken to a hospital where he was declared dead. The prosecution presented eyewitness accounts, medical evidence, and recovery of weapons. The trial court convicted the accused of murder under Section 302 of the IPC, and the High Court upheld the conviction. The accused claimed the case fell under Exception 4 to Section 300, but the Supreme Court rejected this, emphasizing the use of dangerous weapons and the victim's helplessness.

title: PREM KUMAR GULATI versus STATE OF HARYANA AND ANOTHER
case_title: Prem Kumar Gulati v. State of Haryana
neutral_facts: The prosecution case was based on a dying declaration from the victim, who stated that her husband, along with her brother-in-law and his wife, poured kerosene oil on her and set her on fire. The victim also mentioned that her husband had an illicit relationship with his sister-in-law, leading to frequent quarrels and physical abuse. The investigation revealed that the accused brother-in-law and his wife were living separately and were found innocent during the investigation. The victim's daughter, who was eight years old, provided a statement that contradicted the dying declaration, suggesting that the victim's injuries were caused by a falling lamp.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment/ fine under Section 302/498-A read with Section 34, Indian Penal Code
physical_harm: Burn injuries leading to death
number_of_offences: Three offences/counts charged, two finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the dying declaration of the deceased as a truthful and reliable statement, even though it was not in question-answer form, and held that it may form the sole basis of conviction if subjected to close scrutiny and found to be truthful.

title: RAJU DEVADE versus STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: Raju Devade v. State of Maharashtra
neutral_facts: The accused, a man, was involved in an incident where a 18-year-old girl sustained burn injuries. The victim, who was alone at her house, was found in flames by her brother. The police inspector recorded an oral statement from the victim, who implicated the accused in pouring kerosene oil on her and setting her on fire with a match-stick. A dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate, which the victim also made, implicating the accused. The victim was later transferred to another hospital where a different Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration stating the incident was an accident caused by a falling chimney. The victim died in the hospital from burn injuries. The prosecution presented medical evidence and witness statements supporting the claim that the death was due to burns, not an accident. The courts below rejected the defense's theory of accidental death, relying on the victim's statements and medical evidence.
offence_severity: Minimum: Life imprisonment, Maximum: Death
physical_harm: Burn injuries causing 72% burns
number_of_offences: Three counts charged, two upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes, accused planned to kill the victim due to love affair and pregnancy
motive: To end the relationship and keep the victim out of his life
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the dying declarations of the deceased, particularly the first and second ones, which implicated the accused in the crime of murder.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, including the victim's statements and the medical evidence, and found that the prosecution's case was supported by cogent evidence.
trial_duration: {'dates_of_offence': '04.03.1989', 'trial_judgment': 'Not stated', 'high_court_decision': 'Not stated', 'supreme_court_decision': '29 June 2016'}
legal_representation: {'accused': 'Kumar Parimal, Ms. Praveena Gautam', 'state': 'Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar'}
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Convicted under Section 302 IPC', 'high_court': 'Maintained conviction', 'supreme_court': 'Appeal dismissed'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the victim's dying declarations, including the oral statement and the first dying declaration recorded by the Magistrate, clearly implicated the accused in the murder. The courts below correctly rejected the defense's theory of accidental death caused by a falling chimney, as the evidence showed the death was due to burn injuries caused by the accused pouring kerosene oil on the victim and setting her on fire.
defence_argument: The defense argued that the third dying declaration, recorded by the Executive Magistrate, exonerated the accused and stated that the death was accidental, caused by a falling chimney (burning lamp). They contended that the courts below should not have relied on the first two dying declarations due to inconsistencies and the lack of corroboration.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that each dying declaration must be considered independently on its own merit, and the court must satisfy itself which one reflects the true state of affairs. The court also emphasized that a dying declaration cannot be rejected solely because it is not in question-answer form.
precedent_relied_upon: Bhupal v. State of Madhya Pradesh 2002 (2) SCC 556; State of Punjab v. Parveen Kumar 2005 (9) SCC 769; Sudhakar v. State of Madhya Pradesh 2012 (7) SCR 128; Ranjit Singh and others v. State of Punjab 2006 (8) Suppl. SCR 802; Prem Kumar Gulati v. State of Haryana and another 2014 (14) sec 646
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution proved the case of murder under Section 302 IPC, and the courts below correctly convicted the accused based on the reliable dying declarations and other evidence, rejecting the defense's theory of accidental death.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a man, was involved in an incident where a 18-year-old girl sustained burn injuries. The victim, who was alone at her house, was found in flames by her brother. The police inspector recorded an oral statement from the victim, who implicated the accused in pouring kerosene oil on her and setting her on fire with a match-stick. A dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate, which the victim also made, implicating the accused. The victim was later transferred to another hospital where a different Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration stating the incident was an accident caused by a falling chimney. The victim died in the hospital from burn injuries. The prosecution presented medical evidence and witness statements supporting the claim that the death was due to burns, not an accident. The courts below rejected the defense's theory of accidental death, relying on the victim's statements and medical evidence.

title: ARUN RAJ versus UNION OF INDIA AND ORS.
case_title: Arun Raj v. Union of India and Ors.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.69 of Army Act
aggravating_circumstances: Deliberate planning, use of a sharp weapon, striking a vital part of the body
trial_court_outcome: Guilty of murder, sentenced to 7 years imprisonment and dismissed from service
neutral_facts: The accused, an army official, was charged with the murder of his colleague. According to the prosecution, the accused reported to his superior officer that the deceased and another individual had abused him. After making the complaint, the accused went to the barrack with a kitchen knife concealed in his lungi and stabbed the deceased on the right side of his chest while the deceased was sleeping. The eyewitness to the incident was present and witnessed the stabbing. The deceased succumbed to the injuries.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and death sentence
physical_harm: Death caused by a single stab injury to the chest
number_of_offences: Charged with one offence, upheld as one offence
premeditation_planning: Yes, the court found premeditation and planning
motive: To avenge his humiliation at the hands of the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of the case makes it clear that Section 304 (Part II) IPC is not attracted. The nature of weapon used and the part of the body where the blow was struck, which was a vital part of the body, helps in proving beyond reasonable doubt, the intention of the appellant to cause the death of the deceased.
witness_credibility: The High Court found the testimony of PW-1 Paulose who is the eyewitness and PW-3 Havildar Indrpal to whom the dying declaration was given by the deceased, is reliable.
trial_duration: {'dates_of_offence': '22.3.1998', 'trial_judgment': '25.08.2005', 'high_court_decision': '25.08.2005', 'supreme_court_decision': '13.05.2010'}
legal_representation: {'accused': 'K.K. Mani, Ankit Swarup and K, Lakshminarayan', 'state': 'Brijender Chahar, R.Balasubramaniyam, Naresh Kaushik, Anil Katiyar and D.S. Mahra'}
investigation_status: FIR lodged, charge-sheet prepared, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Conviction and sentence passed', 'high_court': 'Writ petition dismissed', 'supreme_court': 'Appeal dismissed'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused caused the death of the deceased through a deliberate act, using a sharp kitchen knife to stab him on the chest, which is a vital part of the body. The accused had time to plan and deliberate, and the weapon used was dangerous enough to cause death. The prosecution contended that the act was intentional and fell under Section 302 IPC, not Section 304 (Part II).
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused acted under grave and sudden provocation due to the deceased's abuse, and therefore, the offence fell under Exception I to Section 300 IPC. They also contended that the single stab injury indicated an absence of intention to cause death, thus making Section 304 (Part II) applicable instead of Section 302.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the intention to cause death is the key factor in determining whether an act constitutes murder under Section 302 IPC. The court emphasized that the nature of the injury, the part of the body struck, and the weapon used are critical in assessing the offender's intent.
precedent_relied_upon: Mancini v. Director of Public Prosecution (1942) A.C. 200; Rex v. Lesbini (1914) 3 K.B. 1116; State of Rajasthan v. Dhool Singh (2004) 12 SCC 546; Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1958 SC 465; Anil v. State of Haryana (2007) 10 SCC 274
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence of life imprisonment was imposed because the court found that the accused had the intention to cause death, and the act was deliberate, not impulsive. The court rejected the defence's argument that the act fell under Exception I to Section 300 IPC or Section 304 (Part II).
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, an army official, was charged with the murder of his colleague. According to the prosecution, the accused reported to his superior officer that the deceased and another individual had abused him. After making the complaint, the accused went to the barrack with a kitchen knife concealed in his lungi and stabbed the deceased on the right side of his chest while the deceased was sleeping. The eyewitness to the incident was present and witnessed the stabbing. The deceased succumbed to the injuries. The accused was initially sentenced to 7 years of rigorous imprisonment and dismissed from service. The sentence was later revised to life imprisonment and dismissal from service. The accused challenged the conviction and sentence, arguing that the incident was due to grave and sudden provocation and that the offense fell under Section 304 (Part II) of the IPC. The High Court rejected these arguments, finding that the accused had sufficient time to deliberate and plan the attack, and that the use of a sharp weapon on a vital part of the body indicated an intention to cause death.

title: JASDEEP SINGH @ JASSU versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: JASDEEP SINGH @ JASSU v. STATE OF PUNJAB
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304 part I and s.34
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 304 part I IPC with life sentence
neutral_facts: The incident occurred at approximately 12:45 a.m. on April 21, 2011, in the area of Baba Rasoi Dhaba, Jalandhar. The deceased was involved in a dispute with the accused, who were his friends. The deceased was found grappling with the accused on a street. The deceased approached the accused, and after a confrontation, A1 took out a gun and shot the deceased. The accused were present at the scene, and there was a fight. The deceased was taken to a hospital, and the accused were later charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
offence_severity: Minimum 10 years, maximum life imprisonment or death
physical_harm: Death caused to the deceased
number_of_offences: Four offences/counts charged; three finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that there was no premeditation and the occurrence took place in pursuance to a sudden fight, but found the evidence of PW13 and PW6 to be unreliable and exaggerated, leading to the dismissal of the conviction of A3 and A4 under Section 34 IPC.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, PW6 and PW13, as unreliable and exaggerated their statements, leading to the disbeliefs of their testimonies. The court also found PW10's testimony to be partially hostile but considered his earlier statement.
trial_duration: The occurrence took place at about 12:45 a.m. on 21.04.2011. The trial court convicted all the accused persons u/s 304 part I of IPC. The High Court concurred with the view of the trial Court. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the High Court confirming the judgment of the trial Court.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused and the State in the Supreme Court: Shekhar Naphade, Siddharth Luthra, Vikram Chaudhri, Sr. Advs., Rajat Bali, Shivram, Gaurav Agrawal, Ms. Aishwarya Dash, Ms. Supriya Juneja, Ms. Shubhangi Jain, Ms. Sonali Sharma, Pankaj Singhal, Yash Giri, Nikhil Jain, Rishi Sehgal, Keshavam Chaudhari, Ms. Ria Khanna, Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Karanvir Gogia, Ms. Shivangi Singhal, Ms. Vamika Gupta, Advs.
investigation_status: Recoveries have been made, including of the weapons. PW24 took up the investigation and completed the formalities.
appeal_history: The trial court convicted all the accused persons u/s 304 part I of IPC. The High Court concurred with the view of the trial Court. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the High Court confirming the judgment of the trial Court. A1 and A2 did not file their appeals. A3 and A4 filed appeals, which were allowed.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused A3 and A4 instigated A1 to shoot the deceased, and that the common intention under Section 34 IPC was established. They relied on the statement of PW6, who initially did not mention the instigation but later improved his statement to include it.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the courts should have disbelieved the evidence of PW6, as it was an improvement to his earlier statement. They contended that there was no sufficient evidence to prove that A3 and A4 were aware that A1 had a gun, and that the prosecution failed to meet the burden of proof under Section 34 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that Section 34 IPC creates a deeming fiction by attributing an offence committed by one to others acting in furtherance of a common intention. The prosecution must prove the common intention to the satisfaction of the court with substantial, concrete, and clear evidence.
precedent_relied_upon: Suresh v State of U.P. (2001) 3 SCC 673; Lallan Rai v. State of Bihar (2003) 1 SCC 268; Chhota Ahirwar v. State of M.P. (2020) 4 SCC 126; Rambilas Singh & Ors. v. State of Bihar (1989) 3 SCC 605; Krishnan & Another v. State of Kerala (1996) 10 SCC 508; Surendra Chauhan v. State of M.P. (2000) 4 SCC 110; Gopi Nath @ Jhallar v. State of U.P. (2001) 6 SCC 620; Ramesh Singh @ Photti v. State of A.P. (2004) 11 SCC 305; Nand Kishore v. State Of Madhya Pradesh (2011) 12 SCC 120; Shyamal Ghosh v. State of West Bengal (2012) 7 SCC 646; Virendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2010) 8 SCC 407
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The incident occurred at approximately 12:45 a.m. on April 21, 2011, in the area of Baba Rasoi Dhaba, Jalandhar. The deceased was involved in a dispute with the accused, who were his friends. The deceased was found grappling with the accused on a street. The deceased approached the accused, and after a confrontation, A1 took out a gun and shot the deceased. The accused were present at the scene, and there was a fight. The deceased was taken to a hospital, and the accused were later charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The trial court convicted all accused under Section 304 part I IPC with life sentences, but the High Court and Supreme Court found the evidence insufficient to establish common intention for A3 and A4, leading to their acquittal.

title: AMRUTLAL LILADHARBHAI KOTAK & ORS. versus STATE OF GUJARAT
case_title: Amrutlal Liladharbhai Kotak & Ors. v. State of Gujarat
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC
neutral_facts: The accused, who were the husband and relatives of the husband of the deceased, were involved in a case where the deceased committed suicide. The deceased was married to one of the accused, and after the marriage, she was subjected to mental torture and harassment due to insufficient dowry. The deceased's father received a call informing him of the incident and arrived at the scene. The police registered a complaint against the accused, and the accused were arrested. During the trial, several witnesses testified about the mental torture and harassment the deceased faced.
offence_severity: Minimum 10 years, maximum life imprisonment or death
physical_harm: The deceased committed suicide, and there was mental torture and harassment leading to her death
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 498-A, 304-B and 306; finally upheld under Sections 498-A and 304-B
premeditation_planning: The court found that the accused subjected the deceased to cruelty, which led to her suicide
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of friends and relatives of the deceased regarding mental torture and harassment by the accused due to insufficient dowry, and the version of the witnesses PW-1, PW-7, PW-8 and PW-9.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their statements were supported by each other and established that the accused were greedy and had started demanding dowry from the date of marriage.
post_offence_conduct: The accused absconded for thirty six days and ultimately surrendered themselves at the Morbi City Police Station.
trial_duration: The trial was held in Sessions Case No.52/2000, with the complaint registered on 23.03.2000 and the trial judgment passed by the Trial Court. The High Court confirmed the order on 17.06.2009, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 26.02.2015.
legal_representation: For the Appellants: K. T. S. Tulsi, Huzefa Ahmadi, Pradhuman Gohil, Taruna Singh, Kuber Boddh, Jaikriti S. Jadeja, Prabuodha Sharma, Charu Mathur. For the Respondent: Nitin Sangra, Hemantika Wahi, Swati Vaibhav, Preeti Bhardwaj, Puja.
investigation_status: Criminal complaint registered as 1-C.R No. 92/2000, investigation carried out, and the accused surrendered on 29.04.2000.
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Sections 498A, 304-B & 306 IPC. High Court: Upheld the conviction. Supreme Court: Dismissed the appeal.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased died by committing suicide within seven years of her marriage and that four witnesses proved that cruelty was meted out to the deceased immediately before her death, leading to the presumption that the suicide was abetted by the accused.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to substantiate the guilt of the accused under Sections 304-B and 306 of the IPC, and that the evidence of relatives and friends of the deceased was not reliable and could not be solely relied upon.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that Sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC are not mutually inclusive, and that a presumption under Section 113-A of the Evidence Act can be raised if certain foundational facts are established and the event occurred within seven years of marriage.
precedent_relied_upon: Ba/want Singh and Ors. v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2008) 15 SCC 497; State of Punjab v. Iqbal Singh and Ors. (1991) 3 SCC 1; Dinesh v. State of Haryana (2014) 5 SCALE 641; Thanu Ram v. State of M.P. (2010) 10 SCC 353
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who were the husband and relatives of the husband of the deceased, were involved in a case where the deceased committed suicide. The deceased was married to one of the accused, and after the marriage, she was subjected to mental torture and harassment due to insufficient dowry. The deceased's father received a call informing him of the incident and arrived at the scene. The police registered a complaint against the accused, and the accused were arrested. During the trial, several witnesses testified about the mental torture and harassment the deceased faced. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC. title: SURINDER SINGH versus STATE (UNION TERRITORY OF CHANDIGARH)
case_title: Surinder Singh v. State (Union Territory of Chandigarh)
aggravating_circumstances: Use of a service pistol, inebriated condition, pointing gun at victim
mitigating_circumstances: No motive or planning, clean record, passage of time, no injury caused
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.307 and Arms Act s.27, sentenced to 3 years rigorous imprisonment
neutral_facts: The accused, a police officer, entered the residential office of the victim in an inebriated condition. After consuming water, he pulled out his service pistol and aimed it at the victim, directing the victim's clerk and steno to leave the room. The accused moved around the table, pulled the lever of the pistol, and prepared to fire. The victim lunged at the accused, causing the bullet to hit the ceiling. The accused attempted to fire again but failed, and a bullet fell from the pistol. The incident was reported to the police, and the accused was arrested. Forensic evidence confirmed that the cartridge recovered from the victim's office was fired from the accused's service pistol. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts, medical reports, and forensic evidence to establish the accused's actions.
offence_severity: Minimum/Maximum: 3 years rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: No injury was caused to the complainant
number_of_offences: Two offences charged, both upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The CFSL Report proves that the cartridge recovered from the office of the complainant was fired from the service pistol recovered from the appellant. The Medico-Legal Report and testimony of the doctor corroborate the ocular versions of the complainant, his clerk, and his steno that the appellant was in an inebriated condition when he entered the residential office of the complainant. Both the complainant and PW-4 have categorically testified that after consuming water, the appellant pulled out his pistol and aimed it at the complainant.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their testimonies corroborated each other and were supported by forensic evidence. The court found the defense's version of events to be 'a patch of lies and figment of imagination' and rejected it entirely.
bail_history: Appellant is on bail, his bail bonds are discharged
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 10th July 1999; Trial judgment: 25th July 2006; High Court decision: 19th May 2010; Supreme Court decision: 26th November 2021
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Jasbir Singh Malik, Ms. Usha Nandini, V, Advs.; Counsel for the State: Manpreet Singh Doabia, Anil Kumar, Sudarshan Singh Rawat, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted and sentenced to 3 years; High Court: Sustained conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, set aside conviction under Section 27 of the Arms Act, reduced sentence under Section 307 IPC to period already undergone
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant, in an inebriated condition, pulled out his service pistol and aimed it at the complainant, thereby attempting to murder him. The CFSL Report confirmed that the cartridge recovered from the complainant's office was fired from the appellant's service pistol. The prosecution maintained that the appellant's conduct was sufficient to constitute an offense under Section 307 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant's version of events was more plausible, suggesting that the complainant had accidentally fired the weapon. They claimed that the complainant had fabricated the incident to avoid criminal liability and that the appellant had no motive or intent to kill.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the doctrine of proportionality in sentencing, emphasizing that the severity of the sentence should be proportionate to the gravity of the offense, considering mitigating factors such as the absence of injury, the appellant's clean record, and the passage of time.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Saleem @ Chamaru & Anr. (2005) 5 SCC 554; Shivaji Genu Mohite v. State of Maharashtra (1973) 3 SCC 219; Bipin Kumar Mondal vs. State of West Bengal (2010) 12 SCC 91; State of M.P. vs. Kashiram & Ors. (2009) 4 SCC 26; Jage Ram & Ors. v. State of Haryana (2015) 11 SCC 366; State of M.P. vs. Kanha @ Om Prakash (2019) 3 SCC 605
sentencing_rationale: The sentence was reduced to the period already undergone due to mitigating factors such as the absence of injury, the appellant's clean record before and after the incident, and the passage of a long time since the offense.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant's clean record, the absence of injury, the passage of a long time since the incident, and his unblemished service record with sixteen good citations.
other_sentence_order: The conviction under Section 27 of the Arms Act was set aside, and the sentence under Section 307 IPC was reduced to the period already undergone. The appellant's bail bonds were discharged.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a police officer, entered the residential office of the victim in an inebriated condition. After consuming water, he pulled out his service pistol and aimed it at the victim, directing the victim's clerk and steno to leave the room. The accused moved around the table, pulled the lever of the pistol, and prepared to fire. The victim lunged at the accused, causing the bullet to hit the ceiling. The accused attempted to fire again but failed, and a bullet fell from the pistol. The incident was reported to the police, and the accused was arrested. Forensic evidence confirmed that the cartridge recovered from the victim's office was fired from the accused's service pistol. The accused claimed an alternate version of events, but the trial court found it dubious. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts, medical reports, and forensic evidence to establish the accused's actions.

title: STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH versus RAKESH MISHRA
case_title: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Rakesh Mishra
statutory_provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act s.13(2), s.13(1)(d); IPC s.120B
trial_court_outcome: Framing of charges against three accused
high_court_outcome: Set aside the order of framing charges
offence_finally_established: Criminal conspiracy, illegal gratification, and misuse of authority
neutral_facts: The accused, including Rakesh Mishra, were involved in granting building and completion certificates to a hotel and club without proper approvals. The original building permission was granted to the applicant, and later a revised plan was submitted. The revised plan involved significant changes from the original plan, including increased built-up area for the hotel and decreased for the club. The accused granted the revision without approval from any committee and accepted honorary membership in the club. The prosecution alleged that these actions constituted illegal gratification and misuse of authority.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 months to maximum 3 years of imprisonment
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Three offences/counts charged, all finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The revised building plan, which was a complete departure from the original plan, and the granting of the completion certificate merely 7 days after the revision of building permission, along with the acceptance of honorary membership, were accepted as key evidence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses by examining the material before it against the prevailing law to reach its conclusions, without commenting on the credibility of specific witnesses.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: Not stated; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 18.05.2007; Supreme Court decision: 23.03.2015
legal_representation: Arvind Varma, Deepika Shari, C. D. Singh for the Appellant; Sumit Kumar Sharma, Niraj Sharma, Brajesh Kumar for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR lodged on 18-01-1998; charge-sheet filed against the three accused persons; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Order of framing charges passed; High Court: Allowed revision petitions, set aside order of framing charges; Supreme Court: Allowed appeals, restored order of framing charges
prosecution_argument: The State argued that the High Court traversed beyond the permissible limit while deciding the legality of the order framing charges, being a pre-trial stage, and that only the charge-sheet along with the accompanying material should be considered at the stage of framing of charges.
defence_argument: The defence argued that G.S. Jadon cannot be held liable for any act/omission done prior to or after his period of service as Building Officer, and that the revision jurisdiction of the High Court also includes the inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of Cr.PC.
legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle that only the charge-sheet along with the accompanying material is to be considered at the stage of framing of charges, so as to satisfy whether a prima facie case is made out, and that it has to be the subjective satisfaction of the Court framing charges.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, including Rakesh Mishra, were involved in granting building and completion certificates to a hotel and club without proper approvals. The original building permission was granted to the applicant, and later a revised plan was submitted. The revised plan involved significant changes from the original plan, including increased built-up area for the hotel and decreased for the club. The accused granted the revision without approval from any committee and accepted honorary membership in the club. The prosecution alleged that these actions constituted illegal gratification and misuse of authority. The High Court set aside the order of framing charges, but the Supreme Court restored the order, finding sufficient material to make out a prima facie case against the accused.

title: UNION OF INDIA & ORS.  versus BODUPALLI GOPALASWAMI
case_title: Union of India & Ors. v. Bodupalli Gopalaswami
statutory_provisions: Army Act, 1950 s. 52(f), s. 63; Pension Regulations for Army (Part I) Regulation 16(a)
trial_court_outcome: Dismissal from service with forfeiture of pension
neutral_facts: The accused, who was the Commandant of a supply depot, was charged with three offenses related to the management of a butchery. The first charge involved the acceptance of meat containing hearts, which were not acceptable parts of carcasses, as part of the dressed meat. The second charge was related to the failure to ensure that required stocks were maintained as reserve in the butchery. The third charge concerned the improper implementation of standard operating procedures for the butchery, resulting in passed animals not being segregated. The accused was found guilty of these charges, leading to his dismissal from service and the forfeiture of his pension.
offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years or such less punishment as is mentioned in the Act (for charge 1) and imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or such less punishment as is mentioned in the Act (for charges 4 and 5(c))
physical_harm: No injuries or death caused
number_of_offences: 3 charges were charged and 3 charges were finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the first respondent made an observation about heart being an edible offal and reiterated it in his report, but noted that there was no evidence he instructed the butchery staff to accept heart as part of dressed meat.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that the Supervisory Officer and Veterinary Officer were charged and punished, indicating their credibility was not in question.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was dated 25.08.2000, the High Court decision was on 22.12.1995, and the Supreme Court decision was on 12.09.2011.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Y. Rajagopala Rao, R. Balasubramanyam, Y. Ramesh, Sureshta Bagga; Counsel for the State: P.P. Malhotra, ASG, Rajiv Nanda, Rahul Kaushik, B.K. Prasad (for B.V. Balaram Das)
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'The High Court partially allowed the writ petition and quashed the order dated 22.12.1995.', 'high_court': "The High Court's order was challenged in Crl. A. prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the High Court erred in quashing the order forfeiting the pension of the delinquent officer, asserting that the President of India has the power under Regulation 16(a) of the Pension Regulations to forfeit pension of an officer dismissed or cashiered by a General Court Martial, independent of the punishment imposed by the court martial.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court was correct in quashing the order forfeiting the pension, asserting that the punishment of dismissal was shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of the offences proved and that the findings of the General Court Martial were not perverse or irrational.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the power to deny pension as a consequence of an officer being cashiered or dismissed vests only with the President of India under Regulation 16(a) of the Pension Regulations, and that the punishment of dismissal is independent of the punishment imposed by the court martial.

title: GANGA SINGH versus STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
case_title: GANGA SINGH v. STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
evidence_type: eyewitness, circumstantial, medical, recovery, dying declaration
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted on the ground that sexual intercourse was with the consent of the prosecutrix
neutral_facts: The accused was prosecuted for rape. The prosecution alleged that the accused committed rape on the prosecutrix. The prosecutrix immediately after returning home narrated the incident to her mother-in-law. One day after the incident, when her husband returned home, she lodged an FIR. The medical report did not give a definite opinion on whether she suffered sexual intercourse, but the FSL report confirmed spots of semen and spermatozoa on her petticoat. The prosecutrix stated that the accused fell her down, covered her mouth, restricted her hands, and committed rape. The FIR and evidence of the prosecutrix's mother-in-law corroborated her statement. The FSL report confirmed sexual intercourse. The accused did not present a defense of consent and claimed he was falsely implicated due to a quarrel with the prosecutrix's husband, but this defense was not supported by evidence.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years rigorous imprisonment / Maximum not stated
physical_harm: Injuries not confirmed, but forensic evidence confirmed sexual intercourse
number_of_offences: One offence charged, one upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The prosecutrix's evidence is reliable and corroborated by the evidence of PW2, the FIR, and the FSL report. The forensic evidence confirms spots of semen and spermatozoa on the petticoat of the prosecutrix.
witness_credibility: The prosecutrix is a competent witness under Section 118 of the Evidence Act and her evidence must receive the same weight as that of an injured witness. Her testimony is corroborated by PW2 and the FIR.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant absconded after the incident and was arrested by the police after ten days.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 21.12.1987; Trial judgment: 30.11.1988; High Court decision: 26.06.2003; Supreme Court decision: 04.07.2013
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Ravi Prakash Mehrotra (Amicus Curiae), Vibhu Tiwari; Counsel for the State: Siddhartha Dave, Jemtiben Ao, Vibha Datta Makhija

defence_argument: The defence argued that the trial court was correct in acquitting the accused as there was no proof of rape, the medical examination did not show injuries, and the prosecutrix omitted to mention the seizure of items in her evidence. The investigation was deemed defective and cast doubt on the prosecution case.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principle that the prosecutrix is a victim and not an accomplice, and her evidence does not require corroboration as it does in the case of an accomplice. The court also emphasized that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the evidence of PW5, corroborated by PW2 and the FIR, established beyond reasonable doubt that the accused committed rape on PW5.

title: ARVIND KUMAR versus STATE OF NCT, DELHI
case_title: Arvind Kumar v. State of NCT, Delhi
mitigating_circumstances: Gross negligence on the part of the appellant led to a loss of human life
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 302 and sentenced to life
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
neutral_facts: The accused, a police guard, was posted at a police station where the victim, a constable, was on duty. The victim was using an official telephone for a prolonged period, which prompted the accused to approach him and request him to end the call. During the interaction, the accused's semi-automatic fire carbine became entangled with the chain attached to his belt, resulting in accidental firing of five rounds. The bullets struck the victim in the neck, leading to his death. The Court concluded the accused's negligence in not keeping the weapon's safety mechanism engaged led to the accidental death, making him guilty of a lesser offense under Section 304A.
offence_severity: minimum/maximum: 2 years imprisonment
physical_harm: Death caused by five bullets in the neck
number_of_offences: Charged under 302, upheld under 304A
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the appellant's semi-automatic fire (SAF) carbine got entangled in the chain of his belt during a scuffle with the deceased, resulting in accidental firing of five rounds of bullets that led to the deceased's death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the version of the prosecution witnesses about the appellant and the sub-inspector making statements does not inspire confidence, while the two eyewitnesses completely support the defence of the appellant of accidental firing.
bail_history: released on bail by this Court by the order dated 27th November 2017
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 28th December 1994; Trial judgment: 02.07.2010; High Court decision: 02.07.2010; Supreme Court decision: JULY 17, 2023
legal_representation: S. Nagamuthu, Sr. Adv., Ms. Prerna Mehta, Adv. for the Appellant; Jayant K. Sud, ASG , Shreekant Neelappa Terdal, Mukul Singh, Rajesh Singh Chauhan, P. V . Yogeswaran, Rajan Kr. Chourasia, S. K. Singhania, Dr. N. Visakamurthy, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: offence under Section 304A was registered; investigation transferred to Crime Branch; chargesheet filed under Section 302 of IPC
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under Section 302; High Court: confirmed conviction; Supreme Court: conviction under Section 302 set aside, held guilty under Section 304A
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant intentionally fired the SAF carbine at the deceased, leading to his death. They relied on the ballistic expert's report and ocular evidence to suggest the appellant had knowledge that the use of the SAF could cause death. They also claimed the deceased had seen the appellant and PW-12 in a compromising position, leading to a grudge and motive for the killing.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the firing was accidental, as the SAF got entangled in the appellant's belt during a scuffle with the deceased. They emphasized that the prosecution failed to prove the existence of motive or intentional firing, and that the version of the prosecution witnesses about the statements of the appellant and PW-12 did not inspire confidence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the doctrine of res gestae under Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act, and considered the principle of gross negligence under Section 304A of the IPC. The court also examined the failure to prove motive and intention under Section 302 of the IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: The court relied on the interpretation of Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act and the principles of culpable homicide under Section 299 of the IPC.
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed due to the gross negligence of the appellant in not keeping the change lever of the SAF in a safety position, which led to the accidental firing and the loss of human life. The court held that the appellant was guilty of a lesser offence under Section 304A of the IPC.
other_sentence_order: The court set aside the conviction under Section 302 of the IPC and held the appellant guilty under Section 304A of the IPC. The appellant's bail bonds were cancelled as he had undergone the maximum sentence prescribed for the said offence.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a police guard, was posted at a police station where the victim, a constable, was on duty. The victim was using an official telephone for a prolonged period, which prompted the accused to approach him and request him to end the call. During the interaction, the accused's semi-automatic fire carbine became entangled with the chain attached to his belt, resulting in accidental firing of five rounds. The bullets struck the victim in the neck, leading to his death. The prosecution initially alleged intentional firing, but the High Court found the motive unproven. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 302, but the Supreme Court overturned that conviction, finding the prosecution failed to establish intent. The Court concluded the accused's negligence in not keeping the weapon's safety mechanism engaged led to the accidental death, making him guilty of a lesser offense under Section 304A.

title: RAJU & ANR. versus STATE OF HARYANA
case_title: Raju & Anr. v. State of Haryana
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 (Part I) read with s.34 IPC
neutral_facts: The accused persons assaulted the deceased during a conflict that arose from a previous incident where the deceased misbehaved with women at a marriage ceremony. The deceased was chased and surrounded by the accused persons near the house of one Om Prakash. The accused persons inflicted fatal injuries on the deceased with knives, resulting in his death. The prosecution case was that the deceased was chased and held by the accused persons, leading to the fatal injuries. The evidence included eyewitness accounts and medical reports indicating the cause of death was shock and haemorrhage due to multiple injuries.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment / Death
physical_harm: Injuries causing death due to multiple stab wounds
number_of_offences: Four counts charged, two upheld
motive: To preserve the honour and dignity of the womenfolk
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the incident was a result of a previous incident of misbehavior of the deceased with womenfolk during a marriage ceremony, and that the assault was an immediate response to preserve the honour and dignity of the womenfolk.
witness_credibility: The court acknowledged the evidence of PW.5 (the complainant) and PW.7 (another eye-witness) but noted that their testimony, while corroborated by the victim's injuries, did not establish common intention on the part of the appellants.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 31st March, 1994; Trial judgment: 30.10.2007; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: February 10, 2010
legal_representation: Rishi Malhotra for the Appellants; Manjit Singh and Kamal Mohan Gupta for the Respondent
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; Trial completed

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased misbehaved with the womenfolk during a marriage ceremony, leading to an altercation where the accused persons assaulted the deceased. The co-accused were armed with knives, and the deceased was fatally injured by them.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no common intention between the appellants and the co-accused to commit murder. The appellants were unarmed and their role in the incident was to chase and hold the deceased, intending to teach him a lesson, not to kill him.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the common intention to commit murder must be established, and the role of the accused must be assessed based on their actual participation in the incident.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the court found that the appellants did not have a common intention to commit murder, and their role in the incident was less severe, warranting a conviction under Section 304 Part I IPC instead of Section 302 IPC.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the context of the incident, which was a result of a previous altercation and the deceased's misbehavior, and the appellants' role in the incident was to chase and hold the deceased, not to kill him.
other_sentence_order: Appellant No. 1's case was referred to the Juvenile Justice Board under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000.

witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including PW13, as credible eye witnesses whose testimony was corroborated by the post-mortem report, indicating their presence and active participation in the crime.

title: CHINNAM KAMESWARA RAO AND ORS. versus STATE OF AP. REP. BY HOME SECRETARY
respondent: STATE OF AP. REP. BY HOME SECRETARY
case_title: Chinnam Kameswara Rao and Ors. v. State of A.P.

The accused were armed with sticks and assaulted the deceased and the injured witness, causing grievous injuries. The deceased later succumbed to his injuries. The incident was a sequel to a previous altercation between the accused and the deceased and the injured witness. The accused were charged with causing death and causing injuries. offence_severity: Death (Section 302) and causing grievous hurt (Section 324) with minimum/maximum punishment as per IPC
physical_harm: Deceased succumbed to injuries; injured witness sustained bleeding injuries
number_of_offences: Charges framed under Sections 302 and 324 IPC; High Court upheld conviction under Sections 302/34 and 324/34

title: JOSE @ PAPPACHAN versus THE SUB-LNSPECTOR OF POLICE, KOYILANDY &  ANOTHER
respondent: THE SUB-LNSPECTOR OF POLICE, KOYILANDY &  ANOTHER
case_title: JOSE @ PAPPACHAN v. THE SUB-INSPECTOR OF POLICE, KOYILANDY
neutral_facts: The accused, a police constable, and his brother were involved in an incident where the accused's wife was found hanging in their home. The prosecution alleged that the accused and his brother murdered the wife, but the evidence did not directly link the accused to the act. Witnesses testified that they found the wife in a hanging posture and called for help, after which the accused and others arrived and cut the saree to bring down the body. The medical evidence did not conclusively establish the cause of death as homicidal hanging.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 10000/-
physical_harm: The deceased was found in a hanging posture with movements, and later declared dead
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged, one upheld
premeditation_planning: The court did not find premeditation/planning
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of witnesses when considered in conjunction with the testimony of the doctor does not link the appellant directly or indirectly with the actual act leading to the unnatural death of the deceased. The medical evidence also does not decisively establish the case to be of homicidal hanging.
witness_credibility: The courts found the testimony of DWI (Cheriyan @ Papputty) to be trustworthy, noting that he was a major with the required maturity in life's perspectives and would not have lied for the appellant, his father, only to see him through, though knowing him to be the real perpetrator of the crime.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 19.9.2000; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: 3 October 2016
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Basant R., Raghenth Basant, M. F. Philip, Kartik Ashok, Abhishek Tiwari (For Senthil Jagadcesan); Counsel for the State: G. Prakash, Jishnu M. L., Mrs. Priyanka Prakash, Mrs. Beena Prakash, Manu Srinath, Nishe Rajen Shonker
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction of appellant under Section 302 IPC; High Court: Sustained conviction; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that suspicion cannot replace proof in criminal cases, and that the prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed due to the conviction under Section 302 of the IPC for the murder of the appellant's wife, but the Supreme Court overturned this conviction due to insufficient evidence and reasonable doubt in the appellant's favor.
