title: PARVEEN KUMAR versus THE STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH
case_title: Parveen Kumar v. The State of Himachal Pradesh
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498A, s.306; Evidence Act s.113A
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.498A, acquitted under s.306
neutral_facts: The accused married the victim, and she gave birth to a male child. The victim filed multiple complaints against the accused for harassment and cruelty. The victim committed suicide by consuming tablets of aluminum phosphide within seven years of marriage. The accused claimed the victim's suicide was due to her own pain and illness, but the court rejected this, noting the suicide note was not properly exhibited and the accused failed to inform the victim's parents immediately after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence showing the victim's suicide occurred within seven years of marriage and that the accused subjected her to cruelty.
offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine / imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine
physical_harm: death caused by consuming tablets of aluminum phosphide-insecticide
number_of_offences: Two offences charged (ss. 498A and 306 IPC), both upheld by the High Court
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the prosecution's evidence that the deceased had committed suicide by consuming tablets of aluminum phosphide-insecticide within two years of marriage and that the appellant had subjected her to cruelty as contemplated in s.498-A IPC.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as not credible, noting that the defense witnesses did not inspire confidence and the appellant's failure to inform the deceased's parents immediately after the incident smacked of guilt.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 10.10.1992 (marriage), 26.09.1994 (death). Trial judgment: 24.02.2000. High Court decision: 16.03.2011. Supreme Court decision: 23 September 2024.

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant had subjected the deceased to cruelty, which led to her committing suicide, and that the deceased had committed suicide within seven years of marriage, thereby triggering the presumption under Section 113A of the Evidence Act.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the deceased's suicide was due to her own intolerable pain and illness, not the cruelty of the appellant, and that the suicide note was not properly exhibited in evidence, and the appellant had not informed the deceased's parents immediately after the incident.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle under Section 113A of the Evidence Act, which allows the court to presume that a married woman's suicide was abetted by her husband or relative if it occurred within seven years of marriage and she was subjected to cruelty.
precedent_relied_upon: Hans Raj v. State of Haryana [2004] 2 SCR 676 : 2004 (12) SCC 257; Naresh Kumar v. State of Haryana [2024] 2 SCR 830 : 2024 (3) SCC 573
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court found the appellant guilty of subjecting the deceased to cruelty and abetting her suicide, which warranted conviction under Sections 498-A and 306 of the IPC.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused married the victim, and she gave birth to a male child. The victim filed multiple complaints against the accused for harassment and cruelty. The victim committed suicide by consuming tablets of aluminum phosphide within seven years of marriage. The accused was initially convicted under Section 498-A of the IPC but acquitted under Section 306. The High Court upheld the conviction under Section 498-A and convicted the accused under Section 306. The accused claimed the victim's suicide was due to her own pain and illness, but the court rejected this, noting the suicide note was not properly exhibited and the accused failed to inform the victim's parents immediately after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence showing the victim's suicide occurred within seven years of marriage and that the accused subjected her to cruelty.

title: STATE OF PUNJAB versus JAGGA SINGH ETC
case_title: State of Punjab v. Jagga Singh etc.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.25; Arms Act s.25

The medical evidence did not support the claim that the deceased's hand was amputated by the accused.

title: S. K. MIGLANI versus STATE NCT OF DELHI

A forensic science laboratory report was obtained to analyze the handwriting on the documents. The accused applied for discharge on the grounds that he was a public servant and that prosecution sanction was required under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
offence_severity: Not stated
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Multiple offences/counts charged, but only one was finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The FSL report was one of the evidences collected by I.O. Its evidentiary value was still to be gone into at the time of trial in the light of the evidences, which may come before the trial court.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the opinion of a handwriting expert is only opinion evidence, which is a weak nature of evidence and could not have been relied in rejecting the claim of the appellant that he has opened the account in exercise of his official duty.

title: DENY BORA versus STATE OF ASSAM

The deceased was shot from point blank range, as confirmed by the post mortem report. The prosecution relied on the testimony of a witness, PW-14, who came forward almost two years and eight months after the incident. The witness claimed to be threatened by the co-accused, but the delay in his statement and the lack of corroboration raised doubts about his reliability. The prosecution also failed to examine the deceased's wife and daughter, who were present at the scene and could have provided crucial evidence.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment
physical_harm: The deceased was shot dead in his clinic, resulting in homicidal death due to bullet injuries.
number_of_offences: The appellant was prosecuted for 8 offences, but only one was finally upheld.
key_evidence_accepted: The post mortem report confirming the deceased was shot from point blank range, establishing the death as homicidal.
witness_credibility: The court found the testimony of PW-14 (the sole eye-witness) to be thoroughly and wholly unreliable due to his delayed statement, lack of corroboration, and implausibility of his claim of being threatened.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was passed on 02.03.2013. The Supreme Court decision was on 27 August 2014.
legal_representation: P.K. Goswami, Vikas Singh for the appellant; Navnit Kumar, Corporate Law Group for the Respondent.

They relied on the testimony of PW-14, who claimed to be the eye-witness, and the post-mortem report indicating the cause of death was due to shock and hemorrhage from bullet injuries.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the sole witness, PW-14, was unreliable due to his delayed statement and the lack of corroboration. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that conviction can be based on the testimony of a single witness provided he is wholly reliable, but if there are doubts about the testimony, the courts will insist on corroboration. State of U.P. (2012) 8 SCR 1219; Sunil Kumar v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) (2003) 3 SCC 169; Namdeo v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 3 SCR 939
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable

title: ELAVARASAN versus STATE REP. BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
respondent: STATE REP. BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE

aggravating_circumstances: Assault on wife and mother, use of weapon, confinement of victims

witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, particularly PW2 (the wife), as credible and reliable, noting that she not only suffered the assault but survived to provide detailed accounts. trial_duration: Not stated

If such intention is absent, the act may be culpable homicide not amounting to murder. However, the court emphasized that the act of causing injury so imminently dangerous that it will in all probability cause death constitutes murder.

sentencing_rationale: The court imposed the maximum penalty prescribed by law to serve as a deterrent against such crimes, especially in bride burning cases, where the guilt of the accused is established beyond reasonable doubt.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court considered the aggravating factor of the crime being a bride burning case, where the deceased died within three months of her marriage, highlighting the societal and moral gravity of the act.

The accused assaulted her with fists and kicks, then poured kerosene over her and set her on fire. The victim suffered severe burns and later succumbed to her injuries. The victim's dying declaration, along with the testimony of her family members and neighbors, established the accused's actions. A post-mortem report confirmed the cause of death as shock and septicaemia from the burns. The accused attempted to extinguish the fire by pouring water on the victim, but this act was not considered a mitigating factor as it was seen as an attempt to conceal his guilt.

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the prosecution must prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and that the testimony of interested and related witnesses must be scrutinized with due care and caution. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the 'crime test', 'criminal test', and the 'rarest of rare test' while awarding the death sentence. The 'crime test' requires the crime to be of the utmost gravity, the 'criminal test' requires no mitigating circumstances, and the 'rarest of rare test' is society-centric and not judge-centric.
